# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **Its caption:** a title and a sentence or two, written from the fact sheet.

A caption says nothing the fact sheet does not say. What a project taught the person, what was wrong before they came, how often a thing is used: those are theirs to tell you. Where you want such a sentence and do not have it, write the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

# Storyboard — Mina Park

Concept A, the job card. The question: **How do you find out what's actually wrong?**

The object: eight pieces from her own work — hub, wheel, bottom bracket, pedal, frame tube, headset, chain, and the Formula Student pedal-box bracket. All but the bracket are real, physical, worked metal. The bracket alone renders as a thin CAD wireframe, because it hasn't been machined yet — that's true, not a style choice.

## The chapters

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Header | Job card — header | The opening | Her name, course, and the question | Parts drift in rusted and loose, settling into a rough grid | Scroll to begin; rail and "skip to contact" are already visible |
| 2. Customer says | Job card — customer says | Who is asking | The bike as bought; the full list once actually looked at | A wheel tags itself "flat"; then all eight settle into the garage-floor grid, each tagged keep / fix / replace | Tap any piece for its real photo and label |
| 3. What I find | Job card — what I find | How she works | The paint comes off; the hub's real fault, hidden under grease | Frame sheds paint on scroll; hub splits to show the cracked flange | Scrub the paint-stripping scroll; tap the hub |
| 4. Parts | Job card — parts | What she works with, and the other two projects | Her tools; the charger and its honest result; the bracket and its unbuilt state | Tool marks appear on the pieces; a ninth small piece (the charger's gear and housing) enters and leaves; the bracket piece enters as a wireframe | Tap the charger or the bracket for their captions |
| 5. What I did | Job card — what I did | What, shown working | Three evenings on a seized bottom bracket | The bottom bracket piece turns, as if a wrench is on it | Tap for the post it's drawn from |
| 6. Test ride | Job card — test ride | What came of it | The bike mostly whole; the bracket still not proven | Pieces assemble into a rolling bike shape; the bracket stays a wireframe, apart from the rest | Nothing new — this beat is about looking |
| 7. Close | Job card — signed off | The answer, and how to reach her | The answer to the question; how to get in touch | The object at rest, whole — the bracket shown solid, as a stated projection of November, not a claim of fact | Email, CV, the Slow Miles link, all live |

## The beats

### 1. Header

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | 1 | Loose, drifting into a rough grid, dull and rust-brown | Bare metal only — nothing printed yet | A fixed top bar: rail dots for chapters 2–7, and a "get in touch" link, visible from the first screen | "Mina Park. Second-year, Mechanical Engineering, Hallam Institute of Technology, Sheffield." / "How do you find out what's actually wrong?" |

### 2. Customer says

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | 1 | The wheel alone, slightly apart from the rest | A handwritten-style tag: "flat" | Nothing else | "Thirty pounds and a flat tyre. Why I bought a bike that doesn't work." |
| 2.2 | 1–2 (scroll fans the grid out) | All eight lie flat, in the same arrangement as her garage-floor photo | Tags: keep / fix / replace. Confirmed so far — frame: fix (paint), hub: fix (cracked flange), bottom bracket: fix (seized) | A real photo of the garage floor, full width, behind the grid | "An inventory. Every part laid out, photographed and labelled: keep, fix or replace." *(To confirm with Mina: her actual keep/fix/replace label for the pedal, headset and chain — not yet given, so these three stay untagged rather than guessed.)* |

### 3. What I find

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | 1–2 (scroll strips the paint) | The frame tube alone, enlarged | A real photo of the stripped frame, paint peeling away as the visitor scrolls | Nothing else | "Stripping forty years of paint. What was under it, and what I won't do again." |
| 3.2 | 1 | The hub alone, rotating, then splitting open | The real photo of the cracked flange | A short line connecting this to the co-op habit | "It was not the rim. It was a cracked flange on the hub, hiding under the grease." |

### 4. Parts

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | 1 | All eight pause, spaced out in a row | Small tool marks appear: lathe marks on the frame tube, mill marks on the bracket | Nothing else | "SolidWorks, MATLAB, some Python. Lathe and mill, from the workshop induction." |
| 4.2 | 1 | A ninth, smaller piece — a gear and a plain housing — enters from the side, sits a moment, exits | No photo given for this one; shown as plain CAD geometry | Nothing else | "Hand-crank phone charger. First-year design module, 2025. A group of four — my part was the gear train and the housing. It worked, badly: four minutes of cranking for one percent of charge." |
| 4.3 | 1 | The ninth piece for the bracket enters and stays, apart from the other eight, rendered as a thin wireframe | The real CAD view of the bracket | Nothing else | "Formula Student, Hallam Racing. Chassis sub-team, since October 2025. Redesigned the pedal-box mounting bracket: 18% lighter, in CAD and in simulation. Machined in November." |

### 5. What I did

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | 1–2 (scroll turns the wrench) | The bottom bracket alone, a wrench-shape turning against it | A real photo of the bottom bracket, mid-repair | Nothing else | "The bottom bracket fought back. Three evenings, one seized cup, and the thing I should have checked first." |

### 6. Test ride

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | 1 | The eight bike pieces assemble into a rolling bike shape, wheels turning; the bracket sits apart, still a wireframe | Real photos where she has them | Nothing else | "The bike, mostly whole. The bracket: 18% lighter on paper, not yet proven — it's machined in November 2026." |

### 7. Close

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1 | 1 | The object fully at rest; the bracket now shown taking its place, solid | Nothing new | Email (placeholder, see below), a CV download, a link to Slow Miles | "Ask what's reported. Check it yourself. Test it. Say plainly if it worked." / contact details |

## Someone with thirty seconds

The first screen (1.1) carries her name, her course, and the question. The fixed top bar carries a "get in touch" link from the very first screen, which jumps straight to the Close. The rail jumps to any chapter without scrolling through the others. A visitor who taps straight to "Parts" or "Test ride" still gets one real proof (the bracket figure, or the charger's honest result) without reading anything else.

## Without the scene

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | The same seven chapters, same order. Fewer pieces animate per beat (the grid shows four at a time, not eight), and the top rail becomes a small expandable list rather than always-visible dots. Tap replaces hover for a piece's label. |
| With reduced motion | Every beat appears already in its settled end-state — no drift, no paint stripping, no wrench turning. The grid is already sorted, the hub is already split, the bike is already assembled. Captions and real photos are unchanged. |
| With no WebGL | No 3D canvas loads. In its place, in the same order: the real garage-floor photo, the real stripped-frame photo, the real cracked-hub photo, the real bottom-bracket photo, and the real CAD screenshot of the bracket. The site reads as a plain photo-and-text page, chapter by chapter. |
| With no JavaScript | A plain HTML page. The seven chapters run top to bottom as ordinary sections, same captions, same photos, rail becomes normal in-page links. Email, CV link and the Slow Miles link all work as plain anchors. |

## The look and the type

**Workshop** (recommended) — ground: warm concrete grey, like the garage floor. Ink: near-black charcoal. One accent: a single oxide-orange, the colour of a job-card sticker or hazard tape, used only for tags ("fix") and the one "get in touch" link. The eight real pieces render as brushed steel and aluminium with worn, oily highlights; the bracket alone renders in thin cyan wireframe lines, so "built" and "not yet built" are never confused.

**Paper job card** — ground: cream, like a carbon-copy pad. Ink: ballpoint navy. Accent: a red-pen line, used only where a fault was found. Pieces render as pencil-line sketches rather than solid metal.

**Night workshop** — ground: near-black charcoal, one work lamp. Ink: off-white. Accent: warm incandescent yellow, where the lamp falls. Pieces are lit dramatically, in and out of shadow; the bracket glows cyan.

I'd choose **Workshop** — it reads as an actual garage in daylight, not staged, and keeps the orange tag colour doing real work (marking "fix," marking the one link that matters) instead of decorating.

Type: one plain, humanist sans for all reading text — captions, the question, the contact details. One separate face for anything printed on the pieces or the tags themselves — a condensed, stamped, stencil-leaning face, the kind an actual parts label or job-card stamp uses. The two are never mixed within one line.

## Everything else the site needs

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page (the rail, skip-to-contact) | Build | Me — needed for the thirty-seconds visitor |
| A page for each project | Never | Me — one continuous job card keeps it from reading as padded; matches "don't make me look like more than a second-year" |
| Every project listed | Build — all three (bike, bracket, charger) | Me — nothing in the material needs leaving out |
| How to reach her, and a CV | Build | Mina asked for this directly (placement reader, two minutes) — email itself is a placeholder until she sends the real one |
| What others say | Never | Mina — no testimonials exist, and she asked that none be invented |
| Languages | Never, English only | Me — nothing in the material suggests otherwise |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | Build, later | Me — needed before launch, left for once the visuals are settled |
| The page for an address that is not there | Build | Me — kept plain, no joke, in her tone |
| A blog | Never — links out to the existing Slow Miles instead | Me — rebuilding it would duplicate what already exists |
| A chat | Never | Me — not asked for, and out of proportion to the site |
| A legal notice | Never, unless a contact form is added later | Me — contact is a plain email link, not a form that collects anything |

## Open before this can be built as planned

1. Her real contact email (and anything else to list).
2. Whether any photo shows the Formula Student car, team branding, or anyone else.
3. Her actual keep / fix / replace label for the pedal, headset and chain (chapter 2.2 leaves these untagged until she says).
4. Anything else she'd rather not have shown.

## What I'm asking for

A yes to this script, or what to change in it. Everything I decided without asking is in `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`, alongside the four open items above. Nothing gets built in this version — building starts only once the script has a yes.

# Storyboard — Mina Park

Concept A, the job card. The question: **How do you find out what's actually wrong?**

The object: eight pieces from her own work — hub, wheel, bottom bracket, pedal, frame tube, headset, chain, and the Formula Student pedal-box bracket. All but the bracket are real, physical, worked metal. The bracket alone renders as a thin CAD wireframe, because it hasn't been machined yet — that's true, not a style choice.

## The chapters

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What you read | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Header | Job card — header | The opening | Her name, course, and the question | Parts drift in rusted and loose, settling into a rough grid | Scroll to begin; rail and "skip to contact" are already visible |
| 2. Customer says | Job card — customer says | Who is asking | The bike as bought; the full list once actually looked at | A wheel tags itself "flat"; then all eight settle into the garage-floor grid, each tagged keep / fix / replace | Tap any piece for its real photo and label |
| 3. What I find | Job card — what I find | How she works | The paint comes off; the hub's real fault, hidden under grease | Frame sheds paint on scroll; hub splits to show the cracked flange | Scrub the paint-stripping scroll; tap the hub |
| 4. Parts | Job card — parts | What she works with, and the other two projects | Her tools; the charger and its honest result; the bracket and its unbuilt state | Tool marks appear on the pieces; a ninth small piece (the charger's gear and housing) enters and leaves; the bracket piece enters as a wireframe | Tap the charger or the bracket for their captions |
| 5. What I did | Job card — what I did | What, shown working | Three evenings on a seized bottom bracket | The bottom bracket piece turns, as if a wrench is on it | Tap for the post it's drawn from |
| 6. Test ride | Job card — test ride | What came of it | The bike mostly whole; the bracket still not proven | Pieces assemble into a rolling bike shape; the bracket stays a wireframe, apart from the rest | Nothing new — this beat is about looking |
| 7. Close | Job card — signed off | The answer, and how to reach her | The answer to the question; how to get in touch | The object at rest, whole — the bracket shown solid, as a stated projection of November, not a claim of fact | Email, CV, the Slow Miles link, all live |

## The beats

### 1. Header

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | 1 | Loose, drifting into a rough grid, dull and rust-brown | Bare metal only — nothing printed yet | A fixed top bar: rail dots for chapters 2–7, and a "get in touch" link, visible from the first screen | "Mina Park. Second-year, Mechanical Engineering, Hallam Institute of Technology, Sheffield." / "How do you find out what's actually wrong?" |

### 2. Customer says

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2.1 | 1 | The wheel alone, slightly apart from the rest | A handwritten-style tag: "flat" | Nothing else | "Thirty pounds and a flat tyre. Why I bought a bike that doesn't work." |
| 2.2 | 1–2 (scroll fans the grid out) | All eight lie flat, in the same arrangement as her garage-floor photo | Tags: keep / fix / replace. Confirmed so far — frame: fix (paint), hub: fix (cracked flange), bottom bracket: fix (seized) | A real photo of the garage floor, full width, behind the grid | "An inventory. Every part laid out, photographed and labelled: keep, fix or replace." *(To confirm with Mina: her actual keep/fix/replace label for the pedal, headset and chain — not yet given, so these three stay untagged rather than guessed.)* |

### 3. What I find

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.1 | 1–2 (scroll strips the paint) | The frame tube alone, enlarged | A real photo of the stripped frame, paint peeling away as the visitor scrolls | Nothing else | "Stripping forty years of paint. What was under it, and what I won't do again." |
| 3.2 | 1 | The hub alone, rotating, then splitting open | The real photo of the cracked flange | A short line connecting this to the co-op habit | "It was not the rim. It was a cracked flange on the hub, hiding under the grease." |

### 4. Parts

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | 1 | All eight pause, spaced out in a row | Small tool marks appear: lathe marks on the frame tube, mill marks on the bracket | Nothing else | "SolidWorks, MATLAB, some Python. Lathe and mill, from the workshop induction." |
| 4.2 | 1 | A ninth, smaller piece — a gear and a plain housing — enters from the side, sits a moment, exits | No photo given for this one; shown as plain CAD geometry | Nothing else | "Hand-crank phone charger. First-year design module, 2025. A group of four — my part was the gear train and the housing. It worked, badly: four minutes of cranking for one percent of charge." |
| 4.3 | 1 | The ninth piece for the bracket enters and stays, apart from the other eight, rendered as a thin wireframe | The real CAD view of the bracket | Nothing else | "Formula Student, Hallam Racing. Chassis sub-team, since October 2025. Redesigned the pedal-box mounting bracket: 18% lighter, in CAD and in simulation. Machined in November." |

### 5. What I did

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5.1 | 1–2 (scroll turns the wrench) | The bottom bracket alone, a wrench-shape turning against it | A real photo of the bottom bracket, mid-repair | Nothing else | "The bottom bracket fought back. Three evenings, one seized cup, and the thing I should have checked first." |

### 6. Test ride

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | 1 | The eight bike pieces assemble into a rolling bike shape, wheels turning; the bracket sits apart, still a wireframe | Real photos where she has them | Nothing else | "The bike, mostly whole. The bracket: 18% lighter on paper, not yet proven — it's machined in November 2026." |

### 7. Close

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | Its caption |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7.1 | 1 | The object fully at rest; the bracket now shown taking its place, solid | Nothing new | Email (placeholder, see below), a CV download, a link to Slow Miles | "Ask what's reported. Check it yourself. Test it. Say plainly if it worked." / contact details |

## Someone with thirty seconds

The first screen (1.1) carries her name, her course, and the question. The fixed top bar carries a "get in touch" link from the very first screen, which jumps straight to the Close. The rail jumps to any chapter without scrolling through the others. A visitor who taps straight to "Parts" or "Test ride" still gets one real proof (the bracket figure, or the charger's honest result) without reading anything else.

## Without the scene

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | The same seven chapters, same order. Fewer pieces animate per beat (the grid shows four at a time, not eight), and the top rail becomes a small expandable list rather than always-visible dots. Tap replaces hover for a piece's label. |
| With reduced motion | Every beat appears already in its settled end-state — no drift, no paint stripping, no wrench turning. The grid is already sorted, the hub is already split, the bike is already assembled. Captions and real photos are unchanged. |
| With no WebGL | No 3D canvas loads. In its place, in the same order: the real garage-floor photo, the real stripped-frame photo, the real cracked-hub photo, the real bottom-bracket photo, and the real CAD screenshot of the bracket. The site reads as a plain photo-and-text page, chapter by chapter. |
| With no JavaScript | A plain HTML page. The seven chapters run top to bottom as ordinary sections, same captions, same photos, rail becomes normal in-page links. Email, CV link and the Slow Miles link all work as plain anchors. |

## The look and the type

**Workshop** (recommended) — ground: warm concrete grey, like the garage floor. Ink: near-black charcoal. One accent: a single oxide-orange, the colour of a job-card sticker or hazard tape, used only for tags ("fix") and the one "get in touch" link. The eight real pieces render as brushed steel and aluminium with worn, oily highlights; the bracket alone renders in thin cyan wireframe lines, so "built" and "not yet built" are never confused.

**Paper job card** — ground: cream, like a carbon-copy pad. Ink: ballpoint navy. Accent: a red-pen line, used only where a fault was found. Pieces render as pencil-line sketches rather than solid metal.

**Night workshop** — ground: near-black charcoal, one work lamp. Ink: off-white. Accent: warm incandescent yellow, where the lamp falls. Pieces are lit dramatically, in and out of shadow; the bracket glows cyan.

I'd choose **Workshop** — it reads as an actual garage in daylight, not staged, and keeps the orange tag colour doing real work (marking "fix," marking the one link that matters) instead of decorating.

Type: one plain, humanist sans for all reading text — captions, the question, the contact details. One separate face for anything printed on the pieces or the tags themselves — a condensed, stamped, stencil-leaning face, the kind an actual parts label or job-card stamp uses. The two are never mixed within one line.

## Everything else the site needs

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page (the rail, skip-to-contact) | Build | Me — needed for the thirty-seconds visitor |
| A page for each project | Never | Me — one continuous job card keeps it from reading as padded; matches "don't make me look like more than a second-year" |
| Every project listed | Build — all three (bike, bracket, charger) | Me — nothing in the material needs leaving out |
| How to reach her, and a CV | Build | Mina asked for this directly (placement reader, two minutes) — email itself is a placeholder until she sends the real one |
| What others say | Never | Mina — no testimonials exist, and she asked that none be invented |
| Languages | Never, English only | Me — nothing in the material suggests otherwise |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | Build, later | Me — needed before launch, left for once the visuals are settled |
| The page for an address that is not there | Build | Me — kept plain, no joke, in her tone |
| A blog | Never — links out to the existing Slow Miles instead | Me — rebuilding it would duplicate what already exists |
| A chat | Never | Me — not asked for, and out of proportion to the site |
| A legal notice | Never, unless a contact form is added later | Me — contact is a plain email link, not a form that collects anything |

## Open before this can be built as planned

1. Her real contact email (and anything else to list).
2. Whether any photo shows the Formula Student car, team branding, or anyone else.
3. Her actual keep / fix / replace label for the pedal, headset and chain (chapter 2.2 leaves these untagged until she says).
4. Anything else she'd rather not have shown.

## What I'm asking for

A yes to this script, or what to change in it. Everything I decided without asking is in `docs/story/decided-for-you.md`, alongside the four open items above. Nothing gets built in this version — building starts only once the script has a yes.

| 4 | **Parts** | Tools, plus the other two projects | Tool marks appear on the pieces; the charger (gear + housing) enters and exits with its honest result; the bracket enters as a wireframe | Tap the charger or bracket for captions |

One gap I left open on purpose: I don't have your actual keep/fix/replace call for the pedal, headset or chain, so chapter 2 leaves those three untagged rather than guessing.

First screen carries your name, course, and the question. A fixed top bar has a "get in touch" link from screen one, jumping straight to Close, and a rail that jumps to any chapter without scrolling through the rest. | Where | What you get |
|---|---|
| Phone | Same 7 chapters, same order. Fewer pieces animate at once (4 at a time, not 8); the rail becomes a small expandable list; tap replaces hover. |
| Reduced motion | Every beat shows its settled end-state directly — no drifting, stripping, or turning. Same captions, same photos. |
| No WebGL | No 3D loads at all. In its place, same order: the real garage-floor photo, the stripped-frame photo, the cracked-hub photo, the bottom-bracket photo, the CAD screenshot. Reads as a plain photo-and-text page. |
| No JavaScript | Plain HTML. Seven sections top to bottom, rail becomes normal anchor links, email/CV/blog links all work. |

## Look and type

**Workshop** (my pick) — warm concrete grey ground, near-black ink, one accent — oxide-orange, used only for "fix" tags and the one contact link. Real pieces as brushed steel with oily highlights; the bracket alone in thin cyan wireframe, so built and not-yet-built are never confused.

Two others considered: a cream **paper job-card** look with ballpoint navy and a red-pen accent, and a **night workshop** look lit by one lamp. Workshop reads as an actual garage in daylight rather than a staged mood, so that's the one I'd build.

Type: one plain humanist sans for all reading text; a separate condensed, stamped/stencil face for anything printed on the pieces or tags — like a real parts label. Never mixed on one line.

## Everything else the site needs

| | Status | Decided by |
|---|---|---|
| Rail / skip-to-contact | Build | Me |
| A page per project | Never | Me — keeps it from reading as padded |
| Every project listed | Build (all 3) | Me |
| Contact + CV | Build | You asked directly |
| Testimonials | Never | You |
| Languages | English only | Me |
| Shared-link preview + icon | Build, later | Me |
| 404 page | Build, plain, no joke | Me |
| A blog | Never — links to existing Slow Miles | Me |
| A chat | Never | Me |
| Legal notice | Never (no form, just a mailto) | Me |

## Still open

1. Your real contact email.
2. Whether any photo shows the team car, branding, or anyone else.
3. Your actual keep/fix/replace call for the pedal, headset, chain.
4. Anything else you'd rather not have shown.

Say yes to this and I'll treat the storyboard as settled — building is a separate step from here, not something I start automatically.
